subject: Zea Platform: throughput gap, surge hedge and dedicated slab proposal
messages:
From: Liam O'Connor <liam@zea.com>
To: aditya_rao@redwood.com
Date: 2027-04-14T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Dedicated sizing — Zea production profile and ask

Hi Aditya,

Thanks for the sync earlier. As promised I'm sharing a short summary of our expected production profile so your team can propose a Dedicated slab and fallback policy. High level:

- Product: Zea Platform — conversational + summarization + nightly batch enrichment.
- Expected steady-state: ~350 concurrent sessions (user-facing chat), average response ~140 tokens.
- Periodic spikes: end-of-month reconciliation and scheduled enrichment windows produce bursts of up to 1,200 concurrent sessions for ~30 minutes.
- Expected average request rate: 6–8 req/s (API calls) per 1,000 users; converting to tokens we estimate steady-state ~11,000 tokens/sec sustained and mid-peak ~42,000 tokens/sec.
- SLO: 95th token latency <= 400ms for user chat flows; background batch can be best-effort with higher latency.

Attached is our token profile export (zea_token_profile.csv) with per-endpoint percentiles and a couple of sample logs. Can your team map this to a Dedicated slab (GPU count / instance class) and a failover to hosted variants if Dedicated reaches a limit?

We'd also like to understand the unit economics for: committed slab, burst capacity, and a conservative runbook for graceful degradation (model fallback, rate-limits, cached responses).

Thanks — Liam
Liam O'Connor
Head of Platform Ops, Zea
liam@zea.com

Liam — thanks, this is exactly the detail we need. Quick confirmation questions so we size conservatively:

1) Steady-state concurrency: is 350 sessions the peak for normal business hours, or a long-tail average?
2) For the end-of-month spikes, are those user-driven interactive requests (need low p95 latency) or asynchronous enrichment jobs behind a queue?
3) Which model family do you expect to serve for chat vs. enrichment (smaller quantized vs. larger-context model)? If undecided, we'll map two model choices and show cost/latency tradeoffs.

Next steps: Stephanie (Solutions) will put together a GPU-slab proposal that converts your token/sec curve into slab counts, plus a recommended safety buffer and fallback policy. Neha will follow up on commercial levers (burst credits and trial). We'll return a packaged recommendation by EOD Friday.

- Aditya

From: stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com
To: aditya_rao@redwood.com, Liam O'Connor <liam@zea.com>
Cc: neha_kapoor@redwood.com
Date: 2027-04-16T08:38:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated sizing — Zea production profile and ask (proposed slab and headroom)

Liam / Aditya — I dug into the token_profile attachment and ran it through our slab modeler. Below is an executive summary and the sizing math (concise). Detailed workbook attached (dedicated-slab-sizing-v1.xlsx).

Executive summary: recommend a Dedicated slab sized to cover the 95th sustained token rate plus a burst hedge for scheduled spikes. We propose an initial committed slab that covers steady-state + 25% safety and an autoscale-burst configuration for the 30-minute peaks.

Assumptions (runtime + model choices):
- Model A (prod chat): rw-3B-quantized (latency-optimized). Effective per-GPU sustained throughput (redwood runtime): ~18,000 tokens/sec (avg conditions).
- Model B (enrichment / long context): rw-13B-quantized. Per-GPU sustained throughput: ~6,000 tokens/sec.
- p95 latency target is primarily driven by model choice + concurrency; our profiling shows rw-3B-quant at your avg request size hits p95 token latency ~320ms at target token/second per GPU below.

Sizing conversion (token/sec basis):
- Steady-state target = 11,000 tokens/sec. If prod uses Model A for chat: 11,000 / 18,000 = 0.61 GPUs -> round up to 1 GPU for baseline. We do not recommend 1 GPU alone because of headroom, redundancy, and multi-tenant placement constraints.
- Recommended committed slab (conservative): 4 x GPU (Model A instances) -> effective capacity ~72k tokens/sec. After subtracting 35% safety and operational overhead, usable capacity ~47k tokens/sec. That comfortably covers steady-state and mid-peak.
- Burst sizing: end-of-month spikes up to 42,000 tokens/sec. With the committed 4 GPUs + autoscale burst to 8 GPUs, estimated peak capacity = 8 * 18k = 144k tokens/sec (raw) -> usable ~94k after safety. This gives ~2x headroom for the 30-minute window and buys margin for slightly larger responses.

Alternative (mixed model): if enrichment uses Model B on a separate slab, sizing for enrichment peaks (assume 20% of spike tokens go to enrichment pipelines) would require 2 x Model B GPUs to keep job latencies reasonable. We can run a mixed deployment: 4 Model A GPUs committed + 2 Model B GPUs committed + burst autoscale across both pools.

Operational playbook (short):
- Primary: Dedicated slab handles all interactive traffic.
- Overflow: if slab utilization > 85% for > 2 minutes, route new interactive sessions to hosted fallback model (rw-3B-managed) with a smaller response token cap and soft-notify users.
- Batch/Enrichment: scheduled jobs prefer dedicated enrichment pool; non-critical work throttles to queue when cluster > 70% to protect interactive SLOs.

Cost notes: committed 4-GPU slab reduces unit token cost substantially vs on-demand burst. Pricing estimations and a 60-day trial credit are included in the attached workbook (Neha will share the commercial terms).

Attachments: dedicated-slab-sizing-v1.xlsx (sheets: assumptions, per-endpoint token mapping, GPU equivalency, costing), SLA-fallback-playbook.pdf (short ops runbook).

If this fits your expectations we'll move to a technical call to lock model choices and run a short 48-hour load test.

- Stephanie
Stephanie Nguyen
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Team — thanks, this is helpful and the headroom math looks reasonable. A couple of follow-ups before procurement signs:

1) Can you confirm the exact p95 testing profile that produced the ~18k tokens/sec per GPU figure for rw-3B-quantized (sequence length distribution, concurrency mix)? I'd like reproducible test steps we can validate.
2) For the autoscale burst pricing: can you provide a rate for burst-to-8-GPU for the 30-minute windows (we'll want predictable amortized cost if we see monthly bursts)?
3) Will Redwood commit to the routing failover described (hosted fallback + cached prefix responses) as a formalized part of the SLA for ZE-4372 trial?

If those answers look good we'll request a 60-day trial slab with the proposed 4 GPU committed + burst enabled to 8 GPUs and proceed to the legal/pricing step.

Liam

Liam — quick answers and next steps:

1) Test reproducibility: Stephanie attached the test harness README inside the workbook (sheet: test-profile). Summary: 90/10 user:system traffic mix, seq length distribution median 120 / 95th 320 tokens, sustained 5-minute ramps. We'll send the exact JMeter/runner commands and container image so you can reproduce locally.

2) Burst pricing: Neha — can you confirm the temporary autoscale rate (list price and a trial discounted rate for ZE-4372)?

3) SLA failover commitment: we will include a trial-level routing SLA: 99.5% availability for interactive routing within region and the failover routing behavior described in the playbook. Formal SLA and fallback commitments will be included in the trial addendum.

Next steps: Neha will send a term sheet (trial credits + burst pricing) and Procurement can sign the 60-day trial addendum. We'll schedule the 48-hour load test once the trial slab is provisioned (we can provision within 48 hours of signed addendum).

Appreciate the quick turnaround — cc'ing Neha and Stephanie to close the loop.

- Aditya
